contract_plain_english: Subtracting one common real shift from every logit leaves every exact softmax component unchanged: g_j is exp(x_j-a) divided by the sum of all exp(x_i-a). Consequently, the exact components sum to 1. The paper uses deviation from this invariant to compare computed fp16 softmax vectors and reports that the alternative formulations look less accurate, but it gives no normalization-error theorem and does not claim that floating-point sums equal 1 exactly. [PDF p. 3, anchor: equation (1.4) and following discussion; PDF p. 17, anchor: softmax-sum discussion]

source_evidence.observation: The exact softmax has components g_j(x) = exp(x_j)/sum_i exp(x_i) for x in R^n and j = 1,...,n. [PDF p. 1, anchor: equation (1.2)]

source_evidence.anchor: equation (1.4) and the immediately following shifting discussion
source_evidence.observation: The paper gives the shifted identity g_j = exp(x_j-a)/sum_i exp(x_i-a), j = 1,...,n, and says the usual choice is a = max_i x_i without making that choice part of the identity. [PDF p. 3, anchor: equation (1.4) and following paragraph]

statement.algorithm_linkage: Equation (1.4) supplies the exact shifted softmax formula. Section 5 then uses the sum-to-one invariant to compare the basic Algorithm 3.1 and its alternative, and the shifted Algorithm 4.1 and its alternative; the qualitative accuracy ranking is experimental rather than part of the algebraic identity. [PDF p. 3, anchor: equation (1.4); PDF p. 17, anchor: softmax-sum discussion]
binders: The input is x in R^n, with softmax component index j = 1,...,n. [PDF p. 1, anchor: equation (1.2)]
A common scalar shift a is applied to every numerator and every denominator term. [PDF p. 3, anchor: equation (1.4)]
The exact denominator in the shifted representation is D_a := sum_{i=1}^n exp(x_i-a). [PDF p. 3, anchor: equation (1.4)]
conclusions: For every component j, g_j = exp(x_j-a)/sum_{i=1}^n exp(x_i-a). [PDF p. 3, anchor: equation (1.4)]
The exact softmax vector satisfies sum_{j=1}^n g_j = 1. [PDF p. 17, anchor: statement that each softmax vector should sum to 1; PDF p. 3, anchor: equation (1.4)]

In the experiments, Figure 3 compares sums from basic Algorithm 3.1 with sums from the alternative algorithm analyzed in Theorem 3.4. [PDF p. 17, anchor: softmax-sum discussion and Figure 3 description]

In the experiments, Figure 4 compares sums from the shifted algorithm analyzed in Theorem 4.3 with sums from its alternative analyzed in Theorem 4.4. [PDF p. 17, anchor: softmax-sum discussion and Figure 4 description]

The paper interprets these figures as further evidence that the alternative softmax algorithms are less accurate than the basic or shifted algorithms. [PDF p. 17, anchor: final sentence of the softmax-sum discussion]
The order along the figures' x-axis is arbitrary and records the order in which the data vectors were generated. [PDF p. 17, anchor: softmax-sum discussion]
constants_and_indexing: Both the numerator index j and denominator index i range over 1,...,n. [PDF p. 3, anchor: equation (1.4)]
The shift is common across all terms and cancels algebraically between numerator and denominator. [PDF p. 3, anchor: equation (1.4)]
The normalization constant is exactly 1. [PDF p. 17, anchor: softmax-sum discussion]
definitions_and_conventions: Equation (1.4) is an exact algebraic representation of the same softmax defined in equation (1.2), not a new function. [PDF p. 1, anchor: equation (1.2); PDF p. 3, anchor: equation (1.4)]
The phrase that a softmax vector should sum to 1 states the exact normalization invariant used to assess computed vectors. [PDF p. 17, anchor: softmax-sum discussion]
The usual numerical shift a = max_i x_i is a recommended implementation choice, not part of the exact normalization identity. [PDF p. 3, anchor: paragraph following equation (1.4)]
error_notions: The exact source claim is equality of the component formula and equality of the component sum to 1. [PDF p. 3, anchor: equation (1.4); PDF p. 17, anchor: softmax-sum discussion]
For computed vectors, departure of the scalar component sum from 1 is used only as an empirical accuracy diagnostic in this passage. [PDF p. 17, anchor: softmax-sum discussion]
The passage provides no quantitative bound relating normalization error to componentwise or normwise forward error. [PDF p. 17, anchor: softmax-sum discussion]
exceptional_values: The exact formulas are stated for real vectors and do not specify IEEE behavior for NaNs or infinities. [PDF p. 1, anchor: equation (1.1) and equation (1.2); PDF p. 3, anchor: equation (1.4)]

The fp16 plots exclude data cases where basic Algorithm 3.1 produced overflow, so the experimental evidence does not cover those exceptional computations. [PDF p. 15, anchor: final paragraph of the fp16 setup]

The surrounding derivation treats a as a real shift; choosing a = max_i x_i is typical but not required by equation (1.4). [PDF p. 3, anchor: equation (1.3), equation (1.4), and following discussion]
